outline.chapter_title: Mathematical Reasoning with LLMs: Motivation and Overview of DeepSeekMath
outline.description: Introduce why math is challenging for LLMs, the limitations of open models relative to closed ones, and how DeepSeekMath advances the state of the art through data, training, and reinforcement learning innovations.
subtopics: Why mathematical reasoning is hard for language models (structure, rigor, long chains)
Closed vs. open LLMs: performance gaps and accessibility (GPT-4, Gemini vs. open models)
DeepSeekMath family and pipeline: Base → Instruct → RL
Key contributions: 120B-token math corpus; GRPO RL algorithm; unified view of alignment methods
Result highlights: 51.7% MATH without tools; 60.9% SC@64; strong multilingual performance
Benchmarks landscape: GSM8K, MATH, SAT, OCW Courses, MMLU-STEM, BBH, MGSM-zh, CMATH, Gaokao tasks, miniF2F

outline.chapter_title: Mining Web-Scale Mathematical Data: Building the DeepSeekMath Corpus
outline.description: Detail the iterative, scalable pipeline that extracts high-quality mathematical text from Common Crawl, including classification, domain mining, decontamination, and multilingual coverage.
subtopics: Seed corpus and classifier: OpenWebMath positives; fastText training with 500K pos/500K neg; key hyperparameters
Deduplication: URL-based and near-dup to reduce Common Crawl size; ranking by fastText score
Selection by quality and scale: token budgets (40B, 80B, 120B, 160B) and performance-driven choice
Iterative domain-guided mining: domain grouping; ≥10% math-hit domains; human URL annotation; 4 iterations
Final dataset: 35.5M pages, 120B tokens; multilingual emphasis (English and Chinese)
Decontamination: 10-gram exact-match filtering (and shorter 3–9-gram exact match) against GSM8K, MATH, CMATH, AGIEval
Quality validation protocol: train a 1.3B model for 150B tokens on MathPile, OpenWebMath, Proof-Pile-2, DeepSeekMath; compare
Findings: higher average quality, better learning curves, and clear multilingual gains
Practical guidance: pitfalls in web mining (boilerplate, math rendering), importance of human-in-the-loop annotation

outline.chapter_title: From Code to Math: Pre-training DeepSeekMath-Base 7B
outline.description: Explain the continual pre-training of a code-first model on a math-centric mixture, design choices, and their impact on reasoning, coding, and formal mathematics.
subtopics: Initialization: DeepSeek-Coder-Base-v1.5 7B and why code pretraining helps reasoning
Training mixture (500B tokens): 56% DeepSeekMath, 4% AlgebraicStack, 10% arXiv, 20% GitHub, 10% general CC (EN/zh)
Optimization details: AdamW, LR scheduling, batch size 10M tokens, 4K context; HAI-LLM framework
Reasoning modes: chain-of-thought (CoT), program-of-thought (PoT) with Python/sympy
Base-model outcomes: strong MATH and GSM8K; surpassing larger Minerva 540B on key tasks
Generalization beyond math: gains on MMLU and BBH; retained coding skills (HumanEval, MBPP)
Formal mathematics: autoformalization on miniF2F via Isabelle with Sledgehammer
Inference practices: sampling, self-consistency, and when tools help most

outline.chapter_title: Supervised Instruction Tuning for Math Reasoning
outline.description: Cover the construction of a large math-specific instruction dataset and the training of DeepSeekMath-Instruct, including CoT, PoT, and tool-integrated reasoning formats.
subtopics: SFT data curation (776K examples): English (GSM8K, MATH, MathInstruct, Lila-OOD) and Chinese K–12 (76 subtopics)
Solution formats: chain-of-thought, program-of-thought, and tool-integrated reasoning
Training recipe: concatenation to 4K context, 500 steps, batch 256, LR 5e-5
Evaluation without tool use vs. with tool integration (Python, sympy)
Comparisons: state-of-the-art open and proprietary baselines (sizes 7B–70B+)
Key results: strong MATH scores without tools; near-60% with tools; competitive against much larger models
Best practices: prompt design for CoT/PoT; controlling tool calls; avoiding leakage

outline.chapter_title: Reinforcement Learning for Math: Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO)
outline.description: Introduce GRPO as a resource-efficient variant of PPO tailored to LLM reasoning, removing the critic via group-relative rewards and enabling outcome and process supervision.
subtopics: Why PPO is costly for LLMs: critic memory, per-token value targets, KL handling
GRPO core idea: group-sampled outputs per question; advantage from group-relative normalized rewards; no critic
Training objective: clipped policy ratio, direct KL regularization to a reference model, unbiased KL estimator
Outcome vs. process supervision: end-of-output rewards vs. step-level rewards and advantage accumulation
Iterative GRPO: updating reward models with replay; resetting reference to current policy
Efficiency and stability: memory savings, variance reduction, and alignment with comparison-trained reward models
Implementation knobs: group size (e.g., 64), LR (policy ~1e-6), KL coefficient (~0.04), max length (≈1024), batch size (≈1024)

outline.chapter_title: A Unified View of SFT, RFT, DPO, PPO, and GRPO
outline.description: Present a common gradient-based paradigm to compare alignment and RL methods, analyze data sources and gradient shaping, and interpret why RL improves math reasoning.
subtopics: Unified gradient template: Data source, Reward function, Algorithm → gradient coefficient
Method mapping: SFT, RFT, DPO (offline); Online RFT (online); PPO/GRPO (online RL)
Online vs. offline sampling: why Online RFT outperforms RFT as training diverges
Gradient shaping: GRPO’s positive/negative scaling vs. Online RFT’s uniform reinforcement of correct answers
Process vs. outcome supervision: finer step-aware signals improve performance
Iterative RL: refreshed reward models and reference policies yield further gains
Why RL works here: improved Maj@K not Pass@K—distribution sharpening boosts voting/self-consistency
Relation to misalignment in SFT and preference alignment literature

outline.chapter_title: Evaluation Methodology and Results Across Domains
outline.description: Systematically present evaluation protocols, benchmarks, and results for English/Chinese math, tool use, formal math, general reasoning, and coding.
subtopics: Benchmarks and setups: GSM8K, MATH, SAT, OCW Courses, MMLU-STEM, BBH; MGSM-zh, CMATH, Gaokao (Cloze/QA)
Without tools: few-shot CoT prompting; sampling and self-consistency
With tools: PoT programs executed in Python with math/sympy; answer extraction and validation
Formal mathematics: miniF2F autoformalization in Isabelle with Sledgehammer
Key results: Base rivals Minerva 540B; Instruct tops open models; RL reaches 51.7% MATH; SC@64 60.9%
Multilingual gains: improved Chinese math performance due to multilingual corpus
General capabilities: MMLU and BBH improvements; coding parity with code-initialized base (HumanEval, MBPP)
Reproducibility and fairness: contamination checks, few-shot choices, tool constraints

outline.chapter_title: Limitations, Practical Guidance, and Future Directions
outline.description: Discuss current shortcomings, deployment considerations, and promising research directions in data, algorithms, and reward modeling for scalable math reasoning.
subtopics: Observed weaknesses: geometry (e.g., triangles, ellipses) and theorem-proving gaps vs. closed models
Few-shot limitations and model scale constraints; zero/few-shot parity
Data biases and ablation insights: code training helps; arXiv-only training shows limited gains (caveats apply)
Efficiency and cost: why GRPO reduces memory vs. PPO; compute planning
Ethical and responsible release: contamination prevention, multilingual equity, reproducibility
Data: broader sources and coverage; improved CC mining; better labeling and filtering
Algorithms: advanced decoding (tree search), efficient exploration, robust RL under noisy rewards (weak-to-strong)
Reward models: generalization beyond in-domain, uncertainty estimation, scalable process reward modeling
